lessons.title: The Lemonade Stand: Why Prices Exist
lessons.summary: Prices come from people agreeing to swap. That is the whole secret.
outline: A price is two people agreeing to swap
Scarcity and desire set the number
The last price is a number, not a truth
Why any of this needs a market
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A trade happens when two people value the same thing in opposite directions and agree to swap.
A price is the number they agreed on, not a fact about what something is worth.
Scarcity and desire push the price to the level where buyers and available supply roughly balance.
The quoted price is a receipt from the most recent trade, so it is history rather than a prediction.
A market is just a place where enough buyers and sellers gather that a swap is almost always possible.
Price and value are different things and can disagree for a very long time.
riskWarnings: Do not confuse price with value

lessons.title: What Is a Stock, Really?
lessons.summary: A share is a tiny slice of a business, and why anyone would sell one.
outline: Why would anyone sell a piece of a good thing?
Market cap: the price of the whole cake
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A share is a small permanent slice of ownership in a business, nothing more mysterious than that.
Founders sell shares to raise money that never has to be repaid, and to turn years of work into cash.
A shareholder owns a claim on profits, a vote, and whatever is left over if the company is wound up.
Shareholders are last in the queue in a bankruptcy, which is why a share can go to zero.
A dividend hands out part of the profits in cash, and the share price usually falls by about the same amount.
Market cap equals share price times the number of shares, and it is the only sensible way to judge a company's size.
riskWarnings: Shares are last in the queue
Share price alone tells you nothing about size

lessons.title: Why Prices Go Up and Down
lessons.summary: More buyers than sellers pushes price up. It is a tug of war, not magic.
outline: The tug of war is made of orders
Urgency is what actually moves price
What makes people urgent: news and expectations
Why the price already knows most of what you know
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Price is a tug of war between buyers and sellers, and the price is where the knot currently sits.
Every trade has one buyer and one seller, so what is unequal is urgency, not headcount.
Price rises when impatient buyers clear out the cheapest sellers, and falls when impatient sellers clear out the highest buyers.
News moves price only to the extent that it differs from what people already expected.
Good news can send a price down if the news is worse than the assumption already baked into the price.
The current price already reflects most public information, so obvious conclusions rarely make money.

lessons.summary: Two different games played on the same field, with different rules and clocks.
outline: The one real difference: where the money comes from
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: An investor is paid by the growth of the underlying business over years; a trader is paid by price movement over minutes to weeks.

The most common beginner mistake is turning a losing trade into an unplanned long-term investment.

lessons.title: Who Is in the Market?
lessons.summary: Exchanges, brokers, market makers, funds and you: who does what.
outline: The exchange: the building and the rulebook
The market maker: the stall that always has oranges
High-frequency firms: the fastest in the room
So who is taking the other side of your trade?
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: The exchange is the venue and the rulebook; its matching engine pairs buy and sell orders and prints the price.
A broker is your licensed access to that venue, and it earns money through commissions, spreads, interest and order routing.
Market makers quote both a buy and a sell price continuously, earning the spread, which is why liquid instruments fill instantly.
Institutions own most shares and must work large orders slowly, which creates much of the trend and volume you will learn to read.
High-frequency firms compete on speed you cannot match, so avoid any strategy that depends on being fastest.
Regulators try to keep the game fair and your money segregated, but they never protect you from a bad trade.
riskWarnings: Do not try to compete on speed

lessons.title: Bid, Ask and the Spread
lessons.summary: There are always two prices. Knowing which one you get is your first edge.
outline: The spread is a real, immediate cost
Why some spreads are tiny and others are enormous
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: There are always two prices: the bid is what you receive when selling, the ask is what you pay when buying.
The ask is always higher than the bid, and the gap between them is the spread.
Buying and instantly selling loses you the spread, so the spread is an immediate and unavoidable cost of demanding speed.
Every position starts slightly underwater, because you buy at the ask and it is valued at the bid.
Liquid, heavily traded instruments have tight spreads because market makers compete; thin ones have wide spreads.
Spreads widen at odd hours, in low volume, in high volatility and around news.
riskWarnings: You start every trade at a loss

lessons.title: What a Chart Actually Shows
lessons.summary: Time on the bottom, price on the side, and a story in between.
outline: Each mark is a period, not a moment
What the shape is telling you
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A price chart is just price history drawn as a picture so your eyes can see patterns your brain cannot see in a list of numbers.
Time runs left to right along the bottom; price runs bottom to top up the side; the far right edge is now.
Each mark on a chart summarises one period of time, not one moment, and you choose how long that period is.
Summaries hide detail, so a calm daily chart can contain a violent hour.
Charts record the past and the present accurately, tell you nothing about the future, and never explain the reason behind a move.
Always identify the symbol, the timeframe and the price range before you form any opinion.
riskWarnings: The chart is not the market

lessons.title: Line, Bar and Candlestick Charts
lessons.summary: Three ways to draw the same data, and why candles won.
outline: The line chart: closing price only
The bar chart: OHLC in one stick
The candlestick chart: the same four numbers, made obvious
One more thing: colour conventions vary
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Line, bar and candlestick charts draw the same underlying price history with different amounts of detail.
A line chart keeps only the closing price, which makes it clean for long-term shape but blind to what happened inside each period.
A bar chart keeps open, high, low and close, with a left tick for the open and a right tick for the close.
A candlestick keeps the same four prices but fills the open-to-close range as a coloured body, so direction is visible instantly.
Candles won because they are faster to read, and the entire pattern vocabulary of trading is built on them.
Colour conventions differ by platform and region; the rule underneath is always close versus open.
riskWarnings: More detail is not always better

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Candlestick
lessons.summary: Open, high, low, close, body and wicks. Every candle is a little battle report.
outline: What each part tells you about the battle
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Every candle is built from exactly four prices: open, high, low and close.
The body is the rectangle between the open and the close, and it shows the net result of the period.
On a bullish candle the open is the bottom of the body and the close is the top; on a bearish candle they swap.
The high is always the very top of the shape and the low is always the very bottom, whatever the colour.
Wicks are records of failed attempts: a long lower wick means the low was rejected, a long upper wick means the high was rejected.
A candle never reveals the order in which the high and low happened, so two very different sessions can look identical.
riskWarnings: A candle hides the order of events

lessons.title: Bullish and Bearish Candles
lessons.summary: Green and red, and what the size of the body is telling you.
outline: The rule that decides the colour
Body size is the strength dial
Wick size is the rejection dial
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A candle is bullish when the close is above the open and bearish when the close is below it, comparing the end of a period with the start of the same period.
Candle colour is not the same as the change since yesterday, and the two can disagree when price gaps.
Body size measures conviction: long bodies mean one side controlled the period, tiny bodies mean the period was a draw.
Body and wick sizes only mean something relative to the recent candles on the same chart.
Long wicks record failed attempts, and a small body with one long wick is the shape most reversal patterns are built from.
Around 40% of candles in a downtrend are still green, so a single candle's colour is a description, not a signal.
riskWarnings: Green does not mean up since yesterday

lessons.title: Timeframes: The Same Market, Many Zoom Levels
lessons.summary: One daily candle contains 390 one-minute candles. Choosing your zoom matters.
outline: One daily candle contains 390 one-minute candles
The same day, two zoom levels
Picking a timeframe for your life
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A timeframe is how much time each candle summarises, and it is the zoom dial on a chart.
One US daily candle contains 390 one-minute candles, 78 five-minute candles or 26 fifteen-minute candles of the identical day.
Lower timeframes keep more detail and more noise; higher timeframes throw detail away to reveal shape.
Higher timeframes carry more weight because more participants and more money contributed to each candle.
Choose a timeframe that matches the attention you can genuinely give, not the one that looks most exciting.
Decide your timeframe before you enter a trade, and never switch zoom levels to make a losing position feel better.
riskWarnings: Noise looks exactly like signal when you zoom in

lessons.title: Gaps: When Price Jumps
lessons.summary: Why the next candle can open far from the last close, and what gaps mean.
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A gap is a hole in the chart where the new candle's range does not overlap the previous one, because nothing traded in between.
Gaps happen mainly because markets close while news does not, with earnings the most common cause for individual shares.
Instruments that trade around the clock, like forex and crypto, gap much less but still gap when liquidity is thin.
Many ordinary gaps eventually get filled, but gaps caused by a genuine change in value may never fill.
A stop loss cannot protect you inside a gap, because price never trades at your level and the order fills far worse.
Check for scheduled events before holding overnight, and size positions so a bad gap is survivable.
riskWarnings: Eventually is doing a lot of work

lessons.title: Linear vs Logarithmic Scales
lessons.summary: Why a 100-point move is not always the same size on a chart.
outline: Why it matters: the same ten points
Long-term charts are where it bites
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A linear price axis gives equal space to equal point moves; a log axis gives equal space to equal percentage moves.
A move from 10 to 20 and a move from 100 to 110 are both 10 points, but one is a 100% gain and the other is 10%.
On long-term linear charts the early years get squashed flat and recent moves look explosive, which misleads the eye.
Log scale usually turns an apparent exponential bubble into a steadier, more honest slope.
Changing the scale changes trendlines, channels and pattern shapes, so pick one and stay consistent.
Use linear for short-term charts and log for multi-year charts or anything where price has multiplied.

lessons.title: The Doji Family
lessons.summary: Standard, long-legged, dragonfly and gravestone doji: indecision in four flavours.
outline: What makes a doji a doji
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A doji has a body that is tiny compared with its range, usually under 5% to 10% of high-to-low.
It means the session ended in a draw, which only matters after a run of one-sided candles.
Dragonfly (long lower wick) is a bullish rejection; gravestone (long upper wick) is a bearish rejection.
Long-legged dojis show violent indecision and often appear at the end of sharp moves.
Wait for the next candle to close beyond the doji before acting, and stop beyond the far wick.
On their own, dojis are near coin-flips; context and confirmation are what give them value.

lessons.title: Hammer and Hanging Man
lessons.summary: Same shape, opposite meaning depending on where it appears.
outline: The hammer: buyers hammer out a bottom
The hanging man: the first crack in a rally
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Hammer and hanging man share one shape: small body at the top, lower wick at least twice the body, little upper wick.
The trend before the candle decides which one it is: hammer after a decline, hanging man after a rise.
The hammer shows sellers attacked and lost; the hanging man shows sellers appeared for the first time but buyers still recovered.
Both need confirmation: a next candle closing beyond the pattern in the predicted direction.
Hammers test around 60% reliable; hanging men more often see the uptrend simply continue, so they need confirmation badly.
Stops go just beyond the long wick, a little further than the obvious tick to avoid stop hunts.

lessons.title: Marubozu, Spinning Top and High Wave

Spinning tops after a trend are traded like dojis: wait for the close beyond the pattern's range.

Volume typically fades into the right shoulder and expands on the neckline break.
The completion trigger is a close below the neckline; a failed retest of the neckline from below is the second confirmation and the tighter entry.
Measured-move target: pattern height (head to neckline) projected down from the break, for example $112 head, $99 neckline gives an $86 target.
Stops go above the right shoulder (conservative) or above the neckline retest (tight), never just above the neckline on the break candle.
The inverse pattern mirrors everything and needs rising volume on the break; a fakeout through the neckline that reverses is a strong signal the other way.
riskWarnings: It only counts after a trend

lessons.title: Double and Triple Tops and Bottoms
lessons.summary: Price tests a level twice or three times and gives up.
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A double top is an M: two failed tests of the same ceiling, completed by a close below the neckline through the trough between them.
A double bottom is a W: two holds of the same floor, completed by a close above the neckline through the peak between them.
Volume is typically lighter on the second test and expands on the neckline break.
Measured-move target: height from the tests to the neckline, projected from the break, for example $108 peaks and a $100 neckline give $92.
Triple tops and bottoms use the same rules, are rarer, and often produce stronger moves, but a fourth test usually means the level is being worn down.
Two touches of a level is a range, not a pattern; the neckline close is what makes it a top or bottom.

lessons.title: Ascending, Descending and Symmetrical Triangles
lessons.summary: Coiling price and the breakout that follows.
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A triangle is converging price action: flat resistance with rising lows (ascending), flat support with falling highs (descending), or both lines sloping (symmetrical).
Ascending usually breaks up, descending usually breaks down, symmetrical usually follows the prior trend but is close to neutral.
Volume shrinks as the triangle narrows and should expand sharply on the break; a quiet breakout is suspect.
The completion trigger is a close beyond the line, and the break should come between half and three-quarters of the way to the apex.
Measured-move target: the widest height of the triangle projected from the breakout point, for example $50 resistance minus a $44 low gives $6, so a break at $50.40 targets $56.40.
Stops go beyond the last swing inside the triangle or beyond the retest, never a few cents inside the broken line.

lessons.title: Flags and Pennants
lessons.summary: Short pauses after a sharp move, and the flagpole target.
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A flag is a shallow, gently counter-trend channel immediately after a steep impulse; a pennant is the same pause coiled into a tiny symmetrical triangle.
No flagpole means no pattern; the pole is where the edge comes from and what supplies the target.
Volume should be heavy on the pole, light inside the pause and expanding on the break.
The completion trigger is a close beyond the flag boundary in the pole's direction.

Stops go just beyond the far side of the flag; a pullback deeper than about half the pole means it is a reversal, not a pause.

lessons.title: Rising and Falling Wedges
lessons.summary: Converging lines that slope: reversals hiding as continuations.
outline: Context decides whether it is a reversal
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: In a wedge both trendlines slope the same way and converge; in a triangle they lean toward each other from opposite directions.
A rising wedge has a steeper lower line and usually breaks down; a falling wedge has a steeper upper line and usually breaks up.
Shrinking volume while price keeps making new extremes is the exhaustion tell that gives the pattern its meaning.

lessons.title: Cup and Handle, Rounding Bottoms and Tops
lessons.summary: Slow, rounded reversals and the handle entry.
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A cup and handle is a long rounded base after an advance, followed by a short shallow dip near the old high; the handle high is the pivot that triggers the trade.
The cup should be a U rather than a V, retrace roughly 12 to 33 percent of the prior advance, and take weeks to months.
The handle must form in the upper half of the cup, drift gently down and show clearly shrinking volume.
The completion trigger is a close above the handle high on volume well above average.
Measured-move target: cup depth added to the breakout, so a $10 cup broken at $50.30 targets $60.30, with the shallower handle-depth target at $53.30 as a first stop.

lessons.title: Measured Moves and Price Targets
lessons.summary: Turning a pattern into a number you can plan around.
outline: Turning a target into a decision
How often targets are actually hit
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A measured move projects the pattern's height from the point where price closed beyond the line, in the direction of the break.
Measure from the pattern's extreme at its widest point, and for flags and pennants measure the pole rather than the pause.
A target is only useful next to a stop: a $6.00 target with a $1.50 risk is a 4R trade, and the R-multiple is what decides whether to take it.
If a significant support, resistance or round number sits in the path, that level is the realistic target, not the formula's number.
Full measured targets are reached in well under half of completed patterns, so scale out at structure and let a remainder run.
Never move the stop to make room for the target; the target is a guess and the stop is the definition of being wrong.

lessons.title: When Patterns Fail
lessons.summary: Failed patterns are signals too, often better ones.
outline: Why the move against a pattern is so fast
Retest or failure? One question settles it
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A failed pattern moves fast because forced exits, a tight cluster of triggered stops and fresh opposite entries all arrive at once.
The difference between a retest and a failure is which side of the level price closes on; wicks are retests, closes through are failures.
The classic trap is four steps: clean pattern, convincing break, close back inside within a few candles, then acceleration to the far side.
Trade it with the close back inside as the entry, the fakeout extreme as the stop and the opposite side of the pattern as the target, which often gives a very high R-multiple.
The most trustworthy failures come from clean, widely watched patterns, reverse quickly, and agree with the higher timeframe.
Never add to the original failed trade or flip without closing it; trade the failure as a new position with fresh sizing.
riskWarnings: Do not flip on every wiggle, and never average into the failed trade

lessons.title: Moving Averages: SMA, EMA and WMA
lessons.summary: Smoothing price to see the trend, and how the formulas differ.
outline: Three ways traders use moving averages
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: A moving average is the average of the last N closes, recalculated on every new candle to smooth out noise.
The SMA weights every close equally; the EMA weights recent closes more using k = 2 / (N + 1); the WMA weights them in a straight line.
Faster averages react sooner but whipsaw more; slower averages are calmer but later. No setting is both.
Common lengths such as 20, 50 and 200 are calendar conveniences that became self-fulfilling landmarks.
Traders use averages as a trend filter, as dynamic support and resistance, and by reading the slope.
Averages lag by design and fail in ranges; use them to confirm structure, not replace it.

lessons.title: RSI: Relative Strength Index
lessons.summary: Measuring momentum on a 0 to 100 scale, overbought, oversold and divergence.
outline: What RSI is trying to measure
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: RSI compares the average size of recent up-moves with recent down-moves and squashes the result onto a 0 to 100 scale.
RS = average gain / average loss, and RSI = 100 − 100 / (1 + RS); RS of 1 gives RSI of 50.
Averages use Wilder's smoothing, so a 14-period RSI reacts slowly and each new day counts for one-fourteenth.
70 and 30 are conventions, not laws; in trends RSI shifts its whole range upward or downward.
Overbought readings in a strong uptrend describe strength, they do not predict a top; the same applies to oversold in a crash.
Use RSI to time entries at structural levels and to spot divergence, not as a stand-alone reason to trade.

lessons.title: MACD

outline: What MACD is trying to measure
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: The MACD line is the 12 EMA minus the 26 EMA; the signal line is a 9 EMA of the MACD line; the histogram is MACD minus signal.
MACD is measured in price units with no fixed limits, so there is no true overbought level and readings cannot be compared across instruments.
The histogram turns first, the signal cross second and the zero cross last; each later signal is slower but more reliable.
Above zero the medium-term trend is up, below zero it is down; many traders only take crosses that agree with the zero-line side.
MACD inherits every weakness of moving averages: lag, whipsaws in ranges, and staying extreme in strong trends.
Use structure for direction and stop placement, and MACD for timing and momentum confirmation.

lessons.title: Stochastic Oscillator
lessons.summary: Where the close sits within the recent range.
outline: What Stochastic is trying to measure
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Stochastic measures where the close sits within the highest high and lowest low of the last N bars, on a 0 to 100 scale.
Raw %K = (close − lowest low) / (highest high − lowest low) × 100; %K and %D are 3-period averages layered on top.
The default 14, 3, 3 is the slow stochastic; the unsmoothed fast version is too noisy for most uses.
It hits 80 and 20 far more easily than RSI, so it gives earlier signals and more false ones.
In strong trends it pins at an extreme for weeks; overbought in an uptrend is a description, not a sell signal.
Take signals only at structural levels and only in the direction of the larger trend.

lessons.title: ATR: Average True Range
lessons.summary: The volatility ruler you will use for every stop loss.

ATR measures volatility in price units and says nothing about direction.
Its main job is scaling: stops at a multiple of ATR and position sizes that shrink when ATR grows.
ATR lags and stays elevated after shocks; it is specific to the timeframe it was computed on.

lessons.title: ADX and Trend Strength
lessons.summary: Is the market trending or chopping? ADX answers without caring about direction.
outline: What ADX is trying to measure
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: ADX measures trend strength on a 0 to 100 scale without regard to direction; +DI and −DI supply the direction.

Below 20 to 25 is a range, above 25 is a trend, above 40 is a strong trend.
Its best use is choosing the right playbook: range tools when low, trend tools when high.
It is doubly smoothed and therefore very late, and a rising ADX is not bullish on its own.
Read structure first and use ADX as the confirming number.

lessons.title: Divergence: When Price and Indicator Disagree
lessons.summary: Regular and hidden divergence, and how to avoid false ones.
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Divergence compares the slope between two price swings with the slope between the two matching indicator swings.

Regular bearish is a higher price high with a lower indicator high; regular bullish is a lower price low with a higher indicator low; hidden bullish is a higher price low with a lower indicator low; hidden bearish is a lower price high with a higher indicator high.

Max drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough fall, here $600 or 3.0R, and it decides whether you can actually stay with a strategy.
Sharpe is reward per unit of wobble: two traders with the same return are not equal if one got there far more smoothly.

lessons.title: Scams, Gurus and Red Flags
lessons.summary: If it promises returns, it is selling you something.
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Anyone promising returns is selling something, because a real edge is more profitable used quietly than sold.
Signal groups fail their own economics, and profit screenshots are trivial to fake with demo accounts, editing or survivorship.
Funded-account challenges combine an aggressive profit target with strict drawdown and consistency rules, and the fees are the firm's real business.
Pump groups use their audience as the exit; the people telling you to buy are the ones selling.
Long-con romance and platform scams show a fake balance, honour small early withdrawals, then demand fees to release your money.
Verify any licence on the regulator's own register, typed in yourself, checking name, number, permissions and contact details against clone firms.

lessons.title: Taxes and Record-Keeping (General Principles)
lessons.summary: Trading income is taxable nearly everywhere. Keep records from day one.
outline: Questions to take to a professional
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Tax rules vary by country and by circumstance, so treat everything here as concepts only and consult a qualified professional in your own jurisdiction.
An unrealised gain is profit on an open position; a realised gain is profit on a closed one, and many systems are built around the closing event.
Many jurisdictions treat long holds differently from short ones, and some distinguish investing from carrying on a trading business.
Losses can often be set against gains and carried forward, so undocumented losses are money left on the table.
Keep every statement, confirmation, fee record, conversion rate and transfer record, downloaded as files, from your very first trade.
Your trading journal already captures most of what you need, and the legal responsibility for an accurate return is normally yours.

lessons.title: From Simulator to Real Money
lessons.summary: The graduation checklist and how to size your first real trades.
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Graduate only with 100 simulated trades, positive expectancy sustained across three months, at least 95% rule-following, a written plan and an automatic journal habit.
Discipline degrades under pressure rather than improving, so rules you break on a simulator will be broken more often with real money.
Real money engages loss aversion, and the classic first-month failure is cutting winners early and letting losers run.
Fund only with money you could lose entirely without changing your life: no borrowed funds, rent or emergency savings.
Start at a quarter to a tenth of your simulated risk or less, for example $10 a trade after practising with $200.
Scale one rung at a time after 30 real trades that keep expectancy positive and rule-following above 95%, and step back down if either slips.

lessons.summary: Books, habits and what to study next.
outline: What to learn next, by style
objectivesFromKeyTakeaways: Fluency comes from repetitions, not from more courses; after this module the loop matters more than the reading.
Six books cover almost everything worth knowing: Schwager and Lefevre for perspective, Douglas and Kahneman for the mind, Murphy and Nison as references.
Study by turning every idea into a checkable rule and testing it yourself on charts before believing it.
Thirty minutes most days beats occasional long sessions, and re-reading early lessons after 100 trades reveals things you could not see before.
Specialise only once you know which style fits your temperament and schedule, then go deep in the areas that style actually depends on.
Reading more while trading less feels like progress and is not; keep the ratio of journal entries to reading hours honest.
